unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 1 of Year 6 Computing at Ehel Academy! This is the biggest and most exciting unit of the whole year. In it, you will learn how to think like a computer programmer and how to build real, working programs that solve real problems. A computer only does exactly what you tell it to do, so the skill you are learning is how to give clear, correct instructions. We call this computational thinking.

This unit has six parts (we call them subunits). Each part teaches you a new tool for your programming toolbox. By the end you will be able to plan a program with a flowchart, build it using the three big building blocks of all programs, tidy your code with sub-routines, plan a bigger project, test it carefully, and even put a program onto a tiny hand-held computer called the micro:bit.

You are learning self-paced. That means you move through this guide at your own speed. You have this written guide, a set of Activities to do on the computer, a Practice & Quiz booklet, and a Reference booklet. Whenever you see an Ask Your AI Tutor box, that is a good moment to open a chat and ask a question in your own words.

outcomes: An evaluation is much stronger when you have success criteria — a clear list of what the program should do to be a success. Without criteria, feedback is vague ('I liked it, but it was a bit small'). With criteria, feedback is useful. Compare these two evaluations of an animation:
Weak (no criteria): 'I really liked the animation. The polar bear did a backflip, but it was a bit small.'

Strong (with criteria): 'The sprites could be improved by making the polar bear bigger and the llama smaller. The text only showed for one second — it should stay for three or four seconds so the user can read it. I liked how a repeat loop was used for the backflip.'
The strong evaluation is better because it checks the program against clear criteria (sprite sizes, text timing, use of loops) and says exactly how to improve.

Everything the user sees and hears is the user experience (sometimes shortened to UX). It does not include the code, because users almost never see the code. Programmers think hard about UX: where the menus go, how the screen looks, which buttons show. Good UX makes a program a pleasure to use; bad UX makes it frustrating.

Systematic means careful and organised, following a sensible method — not just testing at random. To test the rock, paper, scissors game systematically, Zara tests it 15 times: five times entering 'rock', five times 'paper', and five times 'scissors'. Each time she records what happened. The more times a program works correctly, the more confident she can be that there are no bugs.

She also tests with unexpected data. What if the user types bananas, or a number, or a single letter? A well-made program should not crash — it should politely handle input it did not expect, for example by saying 'Please type rock, paper or scissors.' Testing and evaluating never really stop. Have you noticed how apps and devices sometimes ask you to install an update? That is because teams of developers keep improving their programs even after they are released. They fix bugs they missed, and they add improvements to the user experience. When you accept an update, you get their newest and best version. It is always wise to install updates, because they often include security improvements that keep your device safe.

concepts.title: Planning Flowcharts
concepts.explanation: Before a programmer writes any code, they usually make a plan. One of the best ways to plan is to draw a flowchart. A flowchart is a diagram that shows every step of an algorithm. An algorithm is just a set of step-by-step instructions — like a recipe, or the directions from your home to school. You have already met algorithms in earlier years. In Scratch you build an algorithm out of blocks. You can also write an algorithm in words, or say it out loud. A flowchart is one more way to show the same idea, but as a picture. Pictures are easy to follow with your finger, and they help you spot mistakes before you start coding. You always begin at the Start shape at the top. Then you follow the arrow to the next step, and the next, until you reach the End shape. Here is a simple flowchart for making breakfast, written as text so you can read it top to bottom: A simple flowchart shown as text (each | is a connector arrow) If you follow this with your finger, the result is clear: you end up eating breakfast. This flowchart uses sequence only — one step after another, always in the same order. The shape of each box tells you what kind of step it is. This is important: the shape gives information all by itself. Here are the five shapes you must know. The decision shape is the most powerful one. It works just like a conditional statement (IF ... THEN ... ELSE) in code. It asks a question that can only be answered Yes or No, and then the flowchart follows a different arrow depending on the answer. Here is Maya's morning-routine flowchart. Notice the decision: 'Is it a school day?'. Depending on the answer, she takes out different clothes. Is it a school day? --- No ---> Take out your weekend clothes Let us predict the result. If it IS a school day, we follow the Yes arrow: we take out the school uniform, then eat breakfast, then finish. If it is NOT a school day, we follow the No arrow: we take out weekend clothes, then eat breakfast, then finish. Both paths join back together before breakfast. This is exactly how selection works in a real program. So what is the big difference between the breakfast flowchart and this morning-routine flowchart? The breakfast flowchart has only ONE path — everybody follows the exact same steps in the exact same order. The morning-routine flowchart has TWO possible paths because of the decision diamond. Depending on the answer to the question, you take a different route. A flowchart with no decision does the same thing every single time; a flowchart with a decision can behave differently depending on the situation. That is what makes decisions so useful. To predict means to say what you think will happen before it happens. To predict the outcome of a flowchart, you follow every step to the end. Here is a flowchart for fixing a computer that will not switch on: Is the computer plugged into the mains? --- No ---> Plug the computer into the mains Is the power cable plugged into the computer? --- No ---> Plug the power cable in Predict the result if the computer is already plugged into the mains AND the cable is already plugged in: both decisions answer Yes, so we skip straight past both 'plug in' steps and reach the End. The prediction is: the computer should already be working, so we do not need to do anything. People use flowcharts like this in real life to predict things such as which patients might need certain healthcare, or whether the price of gold will rise or fall. Engineers use flowcharts to show how to build machines, and businesses use them to explain how to do a job. A robot that plays chess can be programmed with a flowchart — if you understand the flowchart, you can predict its next move! Shape name — What it looks like · What it means Start or End — Oval (rounded) shape · Shows the very beginning and the very end of the flowchart. Connector — Arrow · Shows the order to follow the steps in. Input or Output — Parallelogram (leaning rectangle) · Getting information from the user, or giving information to the user. Process — Rectangle · An action the program does, such as a calculation.

concepts.title: Programming Constructs
concepts.explanation:
A programming construct is a programming idea you use to build programs. There are three big ones, and almost every program ever written uses them: sequence, selection and iteration. Think of them as the three main tools in your toolbox.

Sequence is the order in which instructions run. In Scratch, blocks run from the top of the stack to the bottom. If the instructions are in the wrong order, the program will not work the way you want. Making breakfast is a sequence: you cannot eat the cereal before you pour the milk!

Selection means choosing which commands to run. A conditional statement is one way to use selection. It tells your program to run one set of instructions OR another set, depending on whether a condition is true or false. A condition is a situation the computer checks, such as 'is the answer less than 10?'.

The clever part is that the program works even though we do not know in advance which number the user will choose.

Iteration means repeating something. In Scratch we call iterators 'repeat' blocks or loops. A forever loop repeats forever. A repeat (10) block repeats a set number of times. Loops are useful because they save you from writing the same block again and again.

concepts.title: Data types
concepts.explanation: Computers organise data into data types. You need three of them in this unit. Integer — a whole number, such as 3. The numbers 3.14 and the word 'three' are NOT integers. You can do maths with integers. Character — a single letter, symbol or number, such as A, !, or 4. Your keyboard is full of characters. Strong passwords mix letters, symbols and numbers. String — two or more characters joined together, such as a word or a sentence. Strings can include spaces and are used for messages. The Scratch say [ ] block needs a string. In Scratch, if you type a string where only an integer is accepted, Scratch changes it to 0. That is why trying to add the words 'three' + 'five' gives 0 — you cannot add two words together like numbers!

concepts.title: Sub
concepts.explanation: A sub-routine is a section of code, separate from the main code, that does one specific job. The clever thing is that you can use it again and again. Programmers use sub-routines to make code easier to read and to avoid writing the same instructions many times. There are two important words. To define a sub-routine means to give it a name and write all its instructions. To call a sub-routine means to use it — like calling a friend's name in the yard and they respond. You can call the same sub-routine many times, and different parts of your program can call it. Imagine a gymnast's routine. A 'handstand' has four steps and a 'forward roll' has three steps. If you wrote out every step every time, the instructions would be enormous. Instead, you define each move once, then just call it: Using sub-routines to keep a routine short 4 Put your feet back on the floor See how short Routine 1 is? The same handstand and forward roll sub-routines could be used in a completely different Routine 2 as well. That is the power of sub-routines: define once, call anywhere. A good quiz game usually needs two variables: one for the score and one for the lives. Here is the exact two-variable algorithm from your textbook, which we will use again in the quiz: An algorithm that uses two variables Trace the result. At the start, Score is 0 and Lives is 3 — this is called initialisation. If the player answers 7, the condition is true, so Score becomes 1 and Lives stays 3. If the player answers 5, the condition is false, so the ELSE branch runs: Lives becomes 2 and Score stays 0. To start with 5 lives, change set Lives to 3 into set Lives to 5. To give 2 points for a correct answer, change change Score by 1 into change Score by 2. The same variable in two different sprites The answer variable is shared, so two sprites can both use it. Leo makes a sprite that asks a question and a second sprite (Maya's sprite) that reacts to the same answer, using a broadcast to connect them: Two sprites sharing the answer variable Trace the result. If the user types basketball, Sprite 1 says 'I love basketball' and then broadcasts a message. Sprite 2 hears the message and says 'basketball is a great sport too!'. Both sprites used the SAME answer variable in their own separate scripts. Sub-routines in Scratch: broadcast and receive Scratch is a block-based language: you drag and drop blocks. To make a sub-routine in Scratch, you use the broadcast [ ] block to send a message, and a when I receive [ ] block to catch it and run the sub-routine. (There is also a 'Make a Block' button that does something similar, in a more powerful way.) Here is Maya's spelling quiz. The user must spell the word 'variable'. Getting it right or wrong each calls a sub-routine: Spelling quiz with two sub-routines Trace the result. If the user types variable exactly, the correct sub-routine runs: a 'Tada' sound plays, the score goes up by 1, it says 'Correct!', and the backdrop changes to Party. If the user types anything else, the wrong sub-routine runs: a 'Clang' sound plays, a life is lost, it says 'Not quite...', and the backdrop turns red. Because these actions are in sub-routines, EVERY question can reuse them — you do not rewrite them for each question. Initialisation means getting everything ready at the start of a program. In a car game, blocks like go to x: (-100) y: (110) and point in direction (90) reset the car to the same starting place every time the green flag is clicked. Here is a car game that uses a sub-routine called 'Off course!': Car game with an 'Off course!' sub-routine and initialisation --- Sub-routine: Off course! --- Trace the result. The car starts at the same place each time (initialisation). The forever loop keeps checking: if the car touches the black edge of the track, it broadcasts 'Off course!'. The sub-routine then says 'Off course!' and puts the car back at the start. If you added a second car for a two-player game, it could call the SAME 'Off course!' sub-routine — no need to rewrite it. Two sprites that affect each other like this are said to interrelate. There is one more big reason to love sub-routines: they make your programs much easier to test and fix. If the same actions were copied into ten different places and you found a mistake, you would have to fix it ten times — and you might miss one. With a sub-routine, that code lives in ONE place, so you fix the bug once and it is corrected everywhere the sub-routine is called. As your programs grow bigger, this becomes one of the most valuable skills you can have.

concepts.title: Interface, prompts and prototypes
concepts.explanation: The interface is what the user sees on the screen: the sprites, the backdrops and the messages. A prompt is a message that shows the program is waiting for input, such as 'Type rock, paper or scissors'. Before building the whole game, programmers make a prototype — a basic first version that users can test and give feedback on. It is much easier to fix mistakes at the prototype stage. People who work on how a program looks are called front-end developers. People who work on the code the user does not see are called back-end developers. Even famous game consoles like the Nintendo DS started life as a prototype! Random means an outcome you cannot predict, like a dice roll. Scratch has a pick random ( ) to ( ) block. Prioritising means deciding what to build first — and it usually makes sense to build the hardest, most important parts first. Zara prioritises (1) the computer's random choice and (2) working out the winner. Here is a common bug and its fix. Zara first wrote three separate IF blocks, each with its own pick random 1 to 3. Because a NEW random number was picked in each IF, the answers did not match up and sometimes nothing was said. The fix is to pick the random number ONCE and store it in a variable:

concepts.title: Evaluating and Testing Programs
concepts.explanation: Building a program is only half the job. Good programmers then evaluate and test their work. Evaluation means thinking about what you like, what you dislike, and how the program could be improved. It is one of the main ways we keep getting better. An evaluation is much stronger when you have success criteria — a clear list of what the program should do to be a success. Without criteria, feedback is vague ('I liked it, but it was a bit small'). With criteria, feedback is useful. Compare these two evaluations of an animation: Weak (no criteria): 'I really liked the animation. The polar bear did a backflip, but it was a bit small.' Strong (with criteria): 'The sprites could be improved by making the polar bear bigger and the llama smaller. The text only showed for one second — it should stay for three or four seconds so the user can read it. I liked how a repeat loop was used for the backflip.' The strong evaluation is better because it checks the program against clear criteria (sprite sizes, text timing, use of loops) and says exactly how to improve. Everything the user sees and hears is the user experience (sometimes shortened to UX). It does not include the code, because users almost never see the code. Programmers think hard about UX: where the menus go, how the screen looks, which buttons show. Good UX makes a program a pleasure to use; bad UX makes it frustrating. Systematic means careful and organised, following a sensible method — not just testing at random. To test the rock, paper, scissors game systematically, Zara tests it 15 times: five times entering 'rock', five times 'paper', and five times 'scissors'. Each time she records what happened. The more times a program works correctly, the more confident she can be that there are no bugs. Here is the testing table she uses: She also tests with unexpected data. What if the user types bananas, or a number, or a single letter? A well-made program should not crash — it should politely handle input it did not expect, for example by saying 'Please type rock, paper or scissors.' Thinking about unexpected data is a key part of good testing. Improving code and software updates Testing and evaluating never really stop. Have you noticed how apps and devices sometimes ask you to install an update? That is because teams of developers keep improving their programs even after they are released. They fix bugs they missed, and they add improvements to the user experience. When you accept an update, you get their newest and best version. It is always wise to install updates, because they often include security improvements that keep your device safe. You can work the same way. When a classmate or your teacher finds something to improve in your program, do not feel bad — the biggest technology companies in the world improve their programs all the time. Make the change, then save your project with a note like 'version 2' or 'version 3', so you can see how your work has grown. One famous online game was released before it had been properly tested. It was full of bugs, players around the world complained, the reviews were terrible, and the company had to give everyone their money back — losing millions. Testing matters! concepts.title: Using Variables with a Physical Device
concepts.explanation: Now for something different: a physical programming device — a small computer you can hold in your hand and program yourself. The one we use is the BBC micro:bit. It has inputs (buttons A and B, a microphone, sensors) and outputs (a grid of LED lights and a tiny speaker). You do NOT need to own a micro:bit Go to makecode.microbit.org (blocks) or python.microbit.org (Python). A picture of a micro:bit appears on the left of the screen. When you run your code, this simulator behaves exactly like a real micro:bit — you can click its buttons with your mouse. Everything in this unit can be done with the free online simulator alone. Every computer, including the micro:bit, follows the IPO model: it takes in data (input), works on it (process), then gives data out (output). For example: you press buttons on a calculator (input), it works out the answer (process), and it shows the answer on the screen (output). All of this happens very quickly. Long ago, computers filled whole rooms, but scientists made them smaller and smaller until the portable game console was born — a little computer you could carry outside and play games on. The micro:bit is like your very own tiny games console: once you download your game onto it and attach a battery pack, you can take your program out to the school yard, just like Sami wants to. The first ever machine that could be called a computer was designed in 1837 by an English mathematician, Charles Babbage. He called it the Analytical Engine. Ada Lovelace, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, was one of the first people ever to write instructions for this machine — which makes her one of the first computer programmers in history! Functions: sub-routines for the micro:bit In Scratch you made sub-routines with broadcast. MakeCode has no broadcast block — instead you use a function. A function is a separate section of code that runs when it is called from the main code, and it can be called many times. It does exactly what a sub-routine does: it makes code clearer, reduces repetition, and makes bugs easier to fix (you only fix the function once). Here is a simple MakeCode function example. Button A shows a heart; button B shows a duck: The very same program can be written in MicroPython at python.microbit.org. This is real, text-based code that runs on the simulator: Trace the result. The while True: loop runs forever. Each time around, it checks the buttons. If you click button A, the function show_heart() is called and a heart appears on the LED screen. If you click button B, show_duck() is called and a duck appears. Pressing the simulator's reset button starts it again. Now for Sami's pocket game. The micro:bit shows a number from 1 to 9. The player guesses whether the NEXT number will be higher (press A) or lower (press B). A correct guess adds to the score; a wrong guess ends the streak. Here it is in MakeCode: MakeCode: 'higher or lower' game using variables, inputs and functions on button A pressed: // A means "I think higher" on button B pressed: // B means "I think lower" And here is the same game in MicroPython, which you can paste into python.microbit.org and run on the simulator: The same 'higher or lower' game in MicroPython
concepts.example: Trace the result. The score starts at 0 and a first number (say 4) shows on the screen. The player presses A because they think the next number will be higher. The program picks a new number, say 7. Because 7 > 4, the guess is correct: the score becomes 1 and a happy face flashes. The new current number is now 7, and play continues. A wrong guess shows a sad face and resets the score to 0. This game uses inputs (buttons A and B), a variable (score and current), selection (the IF checks), and produces output (the number and the face on the LED screen).

workedExamples.solution: 2 (c) iteration. Iteration means repeating, using loops such as repeat or forever.

workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is an integer? (a) 3.14 (b) 7 (c) 'three' (d) hello
workedExamples.solution: 3 (b) 7. An integer is a whole number. 3.14 is a decimal and 'three' is a word (string).

workedExamples.prompt: What does the Scratch join block do? (a) adds two numbers (b) joins two strings together (c) compares two numbers (d) repeats code

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: A decision diamond must always have exactly one Yes arrow and one No arrow leaving it. Both paths should eventually lead to the End.

rules.title: Plan before you code
rules.text: A flowchart or a written algorithm on paper saves you time later. Decompose big problems into small parts and build the hardest part first.

rules.title: Initialise your variables
rules.text: At the start of every program, set your variables (score, lives) to their starting values so old values do not carry over.

rules.title: Sub-routines save work
rules.text: Define a job once, then call it many times. When you need to change it, you only change it in one place.

rules.title: Test systematically
rules.text: Test every case several times, including strange inputs. A bug is a clue, not a failure — fix it and your program gets better.

rules.title: The micro:bit follows IPO
rules.text: Input (buttons, shake) then Process (your code) then Output (LED screen, speaker). You can do it all on the free online simulator.

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: A bug is not a failure — it is a clue. Test one small thing at a time, read your blocks slowly from the top, and ask your AI tutor to help you trace what the program does step by step.

A named box that stores a value that can change, such as a score.
A variable that stores information the user types in.
A symbol that does an action, such as + to add or > to compare.
An operator that compares two values: greater than, less than, equal to.

project.title: Create a Scratch Quiz
project.brief: This is your big project — it brings together everything from the whole unit. Working alone or with a partner, you will design, build, test and evaluate your own quiz game in Scratch. This is the perfect chance to build Maya's spelling quiz idea, or invent your own topic (times tables, capital cities, or world festivals from around the world).
steps: Complete these six steps in order. Each one uses a skill from a different subunit.
Write success criteria (from 1.5). List what your quiz must do — for example: a friendly greeting, at least five questions, a score variable, and a final score shown at the end.
Draw a flowchart (from 1.1). Show the algorithm for one question: ask, check the answer with a decision, then add a point or lose a life.
Create a project plan (from 1.4). Decompose the quiz into parts (welcome, questions, scoring, ending) and decide the order to build them.
Create a prototype (from 1.4). Build a simple first version — just the welcome screen and one working question — and test it.
Develop the program (from 1.2 and 1.3). Add the rest of the questions. Use variables for score and lives, and sub-routines for the 'correct' and 'wrong' actions so you do not repeat code.
Test and evaluate (from 1.5). Test systematically with right answers, wrong answers and unexpected input. Then evaluate against your success criteria and note what you would improve.

Ideas to make it special: different levels with different backdrops; questions that get harder as you progress; different reactions for right and wrong answers; a countdown timer; and sprite animations to celebrate a win.
successCriteria: Task: Write a list of success criteria for a good rock, paper, scissors game. A criterion is something the game MUST do to be a success.
The game welcomes the user and explains the rules.
The computer's choice is random and cannot be predicted.
The program correctly announces the winner for all nine combinations.
The program handles unexpected input politely (does not crash).
The score updates correctly after each round.
Expected result: A clear list you can use to judge any rock, paper, scissors game — your own or a friend's.

selfAssessment: I can an evaluation is much stronger when you have success criteria — a clear list of what the program should do to be a success. Without criteria, feedback is vague ('I liked it, but it was a bit small'). With criteria, feedback is useful. Compare these two evaluations of an animation:
I can weak (no criteria): 'I really liked the animation. The polar bear did a backflip, but it was a bit small.'

I can strong (with criteria): 'The sprites could be improved by making the polar bear bigger and the llama smaller. The text only showed for one second — it should stay for three or four seconds so the user can read it. I liked how a repeat loop was used for the backflip.'
I can the strong evaluation is better because it checks the program against clear criteria (sprite sizes, text timing, use of loops) and says exactly how to improve.

I can everything the user sees and hears is the user experience (sometimes shortened to UX). It does not include the code, because users almost never see the code. Programmers think hard about UX: where the menus go, how the screen looks, which buttons show. Good UX makes a program a pleasure to use; bad UX makes it frustrating.

I can systematic means careful and organised, following a sensible method — not just testing at random. To test the rock, paper, scissors game systematically, Zara tests it 15 times: five times entering 'rock', five times 'paper', and five times 'scissors'. Each time she records what happened. The more times a program works correctly, the more confident she can be that there are no bugs.

I can she also tests with unexpected data. What if the user types bananas, or a number, or a single letter? A well-made program should not crash — it should politely handle input it did not expect, for example by saying 'Please type rock, paper or scissors.' I can improving code and software updates

I can testing and evaluating never really stop. Have you noticed how apps and devices sometimes ask you to install an update? That is because teams of developers keep improving their programs even after they are released. They fix bugs they missed, and they add improvements to the user experience. When you accept an update, you get their newest and best version. It is always wise to install updates, because they often include security improvements that keep your device safe.
